blocks.text: The **hamstrings** are three muscles at the back of the thigh (biceps femoris, semitendinosus and semimembranosus). They extend the hip and bend the knee, and they work hard to slow the lower leg in the late swing phase of running. A **hamstring strain** is a partial or complete tear of the muscle or its tendon, and it is one of the most common injuries in sprinting and kicking sports [Ref - to verify]. Biceps femoris is the most often injured [Ref - to verify].
Two common patterns are described:

rows: Sudden pain during fast running, often in the muscle belly or the musculotendinous junction
Pain during a movement with extreme hip flexion and knee extension, such as high kicking or slides; often nearer the sit bone (ischial tuberosity) and may take longer to recover [Ref - to verify]

blocks.text: A previous hamstring injury is a major risk factor for another [Ref - to verify]. **Proximal hamstring tendinopathy** is a separate, gradual problem causing pain at the sit bone, worse with sitting and running.

items: A sudden sharp pain at the back of the thigh during sprinting or stretching, often with a feeling of a pull or tear, and the athlete stops.
Pain with walking, stairs or sitting, bruising in the first days, and tenderness.
Weakness and pain with resisted knee bending and hip extension.
Proximal hamstring tendinopathy: deep pain near the sit bone, aggravated by sitting, hills, sprints and stretching.

rows: What were you doing when it happened: sprinting, kicking, stretching?
Where is the pain: muscle belly, near the buttock, or at the sit bone?
Did you hear or feel a pop? Could you continue?
Was there rapid bruising or a gap?
Any back pain, buttock pain or tingling down the leg?
Pain when sitting, or gradual onset?
What sport do you play and what is your timeline?

items: Observe bruising, swelling, gait and muscle bulk.
Palpate the muscle belly, the musculotendinous junction and the ischial tuberosity, noting pain, a gap or a hard lump.
Active and passive range of movement: active and passive straight leg raise, knee extension with the hip flexed.
Resisted tests (Section E).
Hip, lumbar and sacroiliac screen and slump test if nerve irritation is suspected.
Functional tests when pain permits: bridge, single-leg bridge, hop and running tests.

blocks.text: Honest note: clinical tests do not reliably grade the exact size of a tear. They help identify the site, severity and readiness to load. MRI is for specific cases, such as suspected avulsion, large tear or slow recovery [Ref - to verify].
E1. Palpation and strength tests

rows: Prone, muscle relaxed, press along the muscle and attachment
Local tenderness, a gap or a lump; pain that reproduces the familiar pain
Prone with the knee bent to 90 degrees; patient pushes the heel toward the buttock against resistance
Pain or weakness suggests muscle involvement
Pain or weakness; more load on the hamstrings in a lengthened position
Prone with the knee straight, lift the leg against resistance
Pain or weakness near the sit bone suggests a proximal injury

blocks.text: E2. Active straight leg raise and passive straight leg raise

rows: The patient lifts the straight leg actively to the pain point, then the therapist raises it passively. Compare with the other side and note where pain begins
Pain and reduced range compared with the other side; pain at a smaller angle suggests more severe injury
A reduced range also occurs from nerve irritation; use the slump test to separate [Ref - to verify]

blocks.text: E3. Askling H-test

rows: Test whether pain or fear of tearing appears in a lengthened position
Supine, the uninjured leg held to the chest
The patient lifts the injured leg quickly toward the ceiling (as if kicking) with the knee straight, to the point of pain or apprehension
Pain, apprehension or a limited, guarded movement compared with the other side
Readiness to return to sprinting when a negative test is combined with other criteria [Ref - to verify]

blocks.text: E4. Bent-knee stretch and Puranen-Orava tests
Tests for the proximal hamstring (sit bone) region:

rows: Supine with the hip and knee flexed; slowly straighten the knee while holding the hip bent
Standing, flex the trunk forward with the knee straight and the foot on a support

blocks.text: Their accuracy is limited and results are interpreted together with history and palpation [Ref - to verify].
E5. Slump test
If sciatic nerve irritation is suspected (tingling, pain spreading down the leg), see Vol 4 Ch 2 for the procedure.
E6. Measures to track
Pain during a standard task, active knee extension range, strength with a handheld dynamometer or tests such as the single-leg bridge, a hop test and sprint readiness [Ref - to verify].

rows: Sudden onset, localised tenderness, pain on resisted flexion
Gradual, sit bone pain, worse with sitting
Sudden severe pain, bruising, gap, unable to walk
Lumbar or sciatic nerve referred pain
Back pain, neurological signs, positive slump
Pain near the sacroiliac joint or deep in the buttock
Pain in a different muscle group
Ischiofemoral impingement or deep gluteal syndrome
Pain with hip extension and adduction

sections.title: G. RED FLAGS AND URGENT CONDITIONS

rows: Sudden severe pain, large bruise, palpable gap, unable to walk, often after a stretch or slide
Protect; refer within days [Ref - to verify]
Severe tense swelling and escalating pain
Numbness, weakness below the knee, foot drop
Back pain with saddle numbness or bladder change
Constant night pain, weight loss, lump

sections.title: H. Working diagnosis and decision pathway

items: Any emergency or urgent flag? **Yes:** act as in Section G.
Suspected avulsion or very large tear? **Yes:** refer for imaging and surgical opinion.
Sudden pain during sprinting or stretching with local tenderness and pain on resisted flexion? **Yes:** working diagnosis is acute hamstring strain.
Gradual sit bone pain with sitting and loading pain? **Yes:** working diagnosis is proximal hamstring tendinopathy; use the tendon loading approach.
Start early graded loading and a criteria-based program.
If recovery is slow or atypical, review the diagnosis and consider imaging and specialist opinion.

rows: Gentle after the first days; avoid direct deep pressure on a fresh bruise
May help if nerve irritation contributes

blocks.text: **Preferred starting choice:** early pain-guided loading and criteria-based rehabilitation. Manual therapy is a minor adjunct. Avoid aggressive stretching of a freshly torn muscle, and avoid deep friction or heavy massage in the first days.

sections.title: J. Exercise prescription (example starting plan, not universal)

blocks.text: **Principle:** begin loading as soon as pain allows, progress by pain-free criteria rather than by time, and rebuild strength in lengthened positions and running mechanics. Programs that include lengthening exercises have been associated with faster return to sport than conventional programs in some trials [Ref - to verify].

rows: Walking, gentle pain-free isometric knee flexion, bridge (two-leg), heel slides
5 holds of 20 to 30 seconds, several times a day
Normal walking pain-free; low pain with isometrics
Bridge progressions (single-leg, feet elevated), hip hinge or Romanian deadlift, slider curl, glute and trunk work
Pain 3 out of 10 or less; no next-day flare
Extender, diver, glider-type exercises (progressive lengthening), Nordic hamstring exercise (when appropriate)

blocks.text: **Symptom rule:** pain up to about 3 to 4 out of 10 during exercise that settles within about 24 hours is generally acceptable. New sharp pain, a new gap or increasing bruising means stop and reassess.

**Return to sport criteria (example):** full pain-free range of movement, strength of at least about 90 percent of the other leg on testing, a negative H-test or similar test, pain-free sprinting at match speed, and sport drills without apprehension [Ref - to verify]. No fixed time is stated, because severity and site differ.

**Prevention:** the Nordic hamstring exercise and similar eccentric programs reduce injury rates in team sports, particularly in athletes with prior injury [Ref - to verify]. Add sprint exposure and manage training load.

**Proximal hamstring tendinopathy:** use progressive loading with isometrics, then bridge and hip hinge progressions, avoiding deep hip flexion stretches and prolonged hard sitting early on. Add running only when sit bone pain settles [Ref - to verify].

**Medical options (decided by doctors):** platelet-rich plasma injections have not shown consistent benefit for acute strains [Ref - to verify]. Surgery is considered for complete proximal avulsions or persistent symptoms.

items: **Visit 1:** screen flags and avulsion signs, explain the injury and expected timeline range, start early loading.
**Early:** pain-guided loading, walking, gentle strength.
**Middle:** progressive strength and lengthening work.
**Late:** running, sprinting and sport drills by criteria.
**Prevention:** continue strength and sprint exposure after return; address lumbar, hip and trunk contributors.
**If slow or atypical:** imaging and specialist input.

blocks.text: Record pain during standard tasks, tenderness on palpation, active straight leg raise and knee extension range, strength tests, H-test, hop and running tolerance.

rows: Pain lowering, strength and range improving
Pain flares and stays worse next day
Plateau beyond expected, or a new gap

blocks.text: **Case:** A 23-year-old footballer felt a sudden sharp pain in the back of his right thigh while sprinting and stopped. There is tenderness in the muscle belly, mild bruising, and pain on resisted knee flexion at 15 degrees. No gap is felt. Walking is possible with mild pain. The H-test is limited by pain. No back or nerve symptoms.

**Working diagnosis:** acute hamstring strain, probably biceps femoris. **Plan:** early pain-guided loading, bridge and hinge progressions, progressive lengthening exercises, graded running and sprint drills, criteria-based return, and a long-term Nordic and sprint exposure plan.
**Questions and answers**

items: Why use criteria instead of weeks? Healing and function differ between people and injuries, so objective criteria are safer than a fixed date [Ref - to verify].
Why check for a gap and for severe bruising? They can indicate an avulsion that may need early surgical review.
A patient has a stretch-type injury near the sit bone and a long recovery. Why? Stretch-type injuries near the tendon tend to take longer to recover [Ref - to verify].
Why add lengthening exercises? Hamstrings often fail in a lengthened position at high speed, so training in that position may improve capacity [Ref - to verify].

How do you tell hamstring pain from lumbar referral? Hamstring pain has local tenderness and pain on resisted flexion, while lumbar referral shows back symptoms and a positive slump with neurological signs.
**Initial approach:** exclude avulsion and nerve problems, then early graded loading.
**Justifying findings:** mechanism, local tenderness, pain on resisted flexion, no gap.
**Priority:** strength, lengthened capacity and running readiness.
**Manual therapy:** minor adjunct.
**Exercise:** isometrics, bridge and hinge progressions, lengthening, running progression, sport drills.
**Modalities:** limited role.
**Tell the patient:** most strains recover well; return depends on criteria; recurrence risk is real.
**Avoid:** aggressive early stretching, deep massage of fresh tears, returning to sprinting before criteria.
**Measure:** pain, range, strength, H-test, sprint tolerance.
**If no improvement:** imaging and specialist review.
**Referral triggers:** Section G.
**Discharge:** return criteria met and a prevention program in place.

blocks.text: **Assumptions:** adult athlete, no avulsion, no nerve injury.

items: **Can be tested:** which rehabilitation approach shortens return and lowers re-injury; whether prevention programs work.
**Hypotheses:** that lengthening exercise improves resistance to injury at high speeds.
**Future questions:** best return criteria and the role of injections.

blocks.text: Evidence not graded until references are verified.

sections.title: Now You Should Be Able To

items: Describe sprint-type and stretch-type hamstring injuries.
Perform palpation, resisted tests and the H-test.
Recognise avulsion and nerve injury.
Build a criteria-based return program.
